title: Knowledge check — 8 questions
note: Unlocks after the applied activity is submitted. Retakes are free and unlimited.

questions.prompt: Why does the module place measurement at position two rather than at the end of the track?
options: Because measurement is the easiest topic and belongs early
Because the most important measurement is taken before the deployment exists, and once it is live the opportunity to observe the before has passed permanently
Because the enablement review in Module 3 is optional
Because baselines take longer to collect than other module activities
questions.explanation: Every other mistake in the track is fixable later. A missing baseline isn't, which is why it is the second module's first lesson rather than the eighth module's footnote.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a baseline from a remembered number?
options: A baseline is expressed as a percentage rather than a count
A baseline is approved by a manager before use
A baseline is a named query against a stated population on a stated date, saved so it can be re-run identically
A baseline covers at least twelve months of history
questions.explanation: Save the query, not just the answer, and write down the population, otherwise the comparison six months later uses a slightly different denominator that happens to flatter the result. That is what happens to everyone who didn't write it down.

questions.prompt: What did IBM's 2018 AskHR mandate demonstrate about activity metrics? `[V]`
options: That mandating adoption is an effective way to drive behaviour change
That usage went to near-universal while HR satisfaction fell from +19 to −35 — so every project-dashboard number improved while the experience got materially worse
That chatbots are unsuitable for HR service delivery
That satisfaction scores are unreliable in HR contexts
questions.explanation: And the collapse was only visible because a pre-mandate baseline existed on a metric measuring experience rather than usage. IBM rebuilt around employees and satisfaction recovered into the +80s, which is why the case is worth teaching rather than just citing.

questions.prompt: Why is self-initiated repeat use the leading indicator this module recommends?
options: Because it is easier to measure than satisfaction
Because it is a revealed preference on a population that could have gone elsewhere — and it is exactly the signal a mandate destroys your ability to read
Because vendors report it as standard
Because it correlates with cost per interaction
questions.explanation: If usage is compulsory, usage tells you nothing. Voluntary return is worth more than any satisfaction survey because nobody is reporting an attitude; they are choosing to come back.

questions.prompt: Where does the rework created by a deployment you run actually land? `[V]`
options: On the deployment team, as botsitting
Nowhere measurable, which is why it can be discounted
On employees, managers and coordinators — none of which appears in the project's numbers, and all of which appears in your queue
On the vendor, under the support agreement
questions.explanation: A is the HRBP track's version, correctly aimed at someone auditing their own workflow. Yours relocates onto people who aren't you, which makes your ticket queue the function's rework detector, and you're the only person who can read it.

questions.prompt: What did the two AI coaching trials establish? `[V]`
options: That AI coaching does not work
That newer models perform worse than earlier ones on coaching tasks
That the same class of technology produced opposite results four years apart, and the variable that changed was task scope rather than the technology
That human coaches outperform AI on every measured outcome
questions.explanation: The 2022 trial gave the AI a narrow structured goal-attainment protocol and it performed comparably to human coaches; the 2026 trial removed the guardrails for open-ended development work and found no significant benefit. One researcher co-authored both, which is what makes the pair trustworthy.

questions.prompt: Why does a broadly scoped pilot tend to be unfalsifiable?
options: Because broad pilots involve more stakeholders who disagree about success
Because a scope wide enough to be impressive is usually wide enough that no specific observable outcome could disconfirm it
Because broad pilots take longer than the evaluation window allows
Because vendors refuse to define success criteria for large deployments
questions.explanation: Which is why the design rule runs the other way: narrow the scope until it works, rather than widening it until it fails. The two questions are what is the single task, and what would failure look like on it.

questions.prompt: Which part of a kill condition does the module say people most often skip?
options: The threshold, because it requires a baseline
The date, because calendars slip
The named person, because teams are easier to assign
A rollback somebody has actually performed — not a documented one, a performed one, with the time it took written down
questions.explanation: An untested rollback is a hope. And the test for whether the whole condition is real is whether it could fire while the sponsor still wants the project; if not, it is a review date with a number attached.
